title: Bidirectional BFS in Seongsu-dong: double the speed!
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS find a route on real street-map style grids by expanding from both start and goal simultaneously. When the two frontiers meet, the shortest path emerges with far fewer explored nodes than one-way BFS.
ig_caption:
🚦✨ Seongsu-dong streets meet graph theory!

In this visualization, **Bidirectional BFS** runs two synchronized breadth-first searches: one frontier expands outward from the **start**, and another expands from the **goal**. Because BFS explores in increasing distance layers, the first time the two visited regions intersect, we can reconstruct a **shortest path** (in an unweighted graph) with impressive efficiency. 🧠📍

On a real street-map graph, intersections are nodes and street segments are edges—so each layer represents “N steps of travel.” Bidirectional search cuts the search space roughly from O(b^d) to about O(b^(d/2)) in typical branching scenarios, where b is the branching factor and d is the path length. ⚡️

fb_caption:
🚶‍♂️💡 Teaching graph search with **Bidirectional BFS**!

We model the district as a graph: intersections = nodes, road segments = edges. **Bidirectional BFS** launches from both the start and destination at the same time, layer by layer, and stops the moment the frontiers meet—guaranteeing a shortest route in an unweighted map.

yt_description:
Seongsu-dong Seoul pathfinding demo using **Bidirectional BFS**! 🚦

In this YouTube Shorts visualization, we convert a street-map style grid into a graph (nodes = intersections, edges = roads) and run **Bidirectional BFS** by expanding from start + goal simultaneously. When the two BFS frontiers meet, we reconstruct the shortest path efficiently—showing why bidirectional search can dramatically reduce explored states.
